claimVerdicts.note: p2 methods match verbatim: four elements "(movement quality, physical conditioning, soccer-specific skills, and training load)" and stage transitions driven by drills, tissue response "along with defined stage-specific criteria".

p1 abstract: "Case series; Level of evidence, 4", 97 followed, 84% RTC (100% pro, 80% amateur), 10 ACL reinjuries. Inclusion required surgeon and physician clearance to RTC (p2), which the brief does not mention but which does not change the claim.
p1 abstract percentages match exactly; the same sentence adds that workloads were lower than match play (TD 44%, DEC 26%), which C20 carries.
p8 verbatim; the authors attribute non-transfer to the different training and match demands of women's soccer.
p8 key point verbatim; case is a 23-year-old professional international central defender (p1).
p3 text matches, including "important (but not unique) criterion" and benchmarks attributed to ref 15. The report does not say what the percentages are relative to, and the claim says so.
p6: "transient episodes of knee pain (as a consequence of the meniscus surgery) delayed the return to running".
p8 key point: IMU analytics "add invaluable sport-specific information ... that can be used to guide phase progression and day-to-day programming". Authors' opinion from one case, framed as such.
p8: "continuous and parallel collaboration that is always required within the multidisciplinary team" in the context of the last conditioning phases.

p3 text matches. This is the authors' general description of RTT/RTC practice; at writing the player had only finished OFR (p1), and the claim's "describes" wording is accurate.

p6-7 match: asymmetry beyond usual day-to-day variability, associated with right knee pain, a few days off running, and both resolved on a softer pitch. Authors add that the reason and direction of asymmetries "are always difficult to understand".
p7 key point verbatim.

p14, p18, p21 table rows match (Kew 2022, Paterno 2021, Welling 2020). Omitted context: Kew and Paterno are adolescent cohorts (mean age 16.1 and 17.2), and Paterno's "confident" is defined by IKDC/KOOS-QOL.
p18 Nyland 2020 row verbatim; framed as a single study summarized in the review, design not given.
p25 text: Domb et al. survey of 27 surgeons at high-volume hip arthroscopy centers; 85% figure and pain-free motions match.

p19 Simon 2020 (n=236, mean age 15.7, mostly ankle sprains): hop distance fell in both limbs, symmetry unchanged. p17 Nagai 2019: isokinetic testing gives "significantly lower LSI values than hop testing", which matches.
p23 text verbatim ("reduced THD LSI even in the cleared athletes").
p14 Kim 2013 row (n=27 healthy): fixation of HHD in supine "increases the reliability and validity".

statementIssues.note: "Published on-field programs ... advance using how the tissues respond" generalizes from one series applying one framework (C1); "passing symmetry-based tests" labels the Paterno and Welling criteria as symmetry-based, but the table summaries do not say so.
Same "symmetry-based criteria" inference as bottomLine; the evidence is three one-line table summaries, two from adolescent cohorts.
The Lisfranc return criterion is the surgeon's protocol described in Methods, not a tested result, and the action presents it as an outcome.

"In the later return-to-train phase, the case report describes partial team sessions" could read as this player's experience; the source describes general practice, and the player had not yet started return to train.

tierNote: Limited is correct. No source tests a combined progression rule or entry criteria for modified practice. The direct evidence is one level 4 male soccer case series and one case report, and the other sources are indirect or digest abstracts. No recommendedDirection is given, and the options are framed as alternatives.
usefulnessNote: Gives a performance or rehab practitioner a clear structure: staged criteria with tissue response, symptom-led holds, separate strength, hop and movement-quality signals, and modified practice as the place for cutting and deceleration exposure. It is candid that no weighting rule exists and that the evidence is male soccer ACL. The text is dense and slightly long for a two-minute read, but the coverage gaps say plainly what is missing.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When a claim's excerpt comes from a Methods or protocol section, label it as the study's procedure or criterion rather than an observed result.

When synthesizing across table-row summaries, do not attach a mechanism label (for example 'symmetry-based') that the rows do not state; carry the population age (adolescent vs adult) for each row used.
Avoid pluralizing a single study's procedure into 'published programs' in the bottom line.
When a case report describes general practice for a later phase the case had not reached, say it is the authors' described approach rather than the case's course.
